summary: 80 ft light steel tower built 1922 for the Tweed Fire District; the district's towers were decommissioned in the 1970s. No source describes the site today.

facts.agency: Former Ontario Department of Lands and Forests (now the MNR), which founded the Tweed Fire District

events.note: Fan-site list of Tweed Fire District towers gives Wicklow as 80 ft light steel, built 1922
Wikipedia gives only the decade: in the 1970s all the Tweed district towers were decommissioned as aerial firefighting took over
Appears on Pembroke topographic map 31F, 3rd ed. (per firelookout.ca)

evidence.supports: Wicklow is in the Tweed district list as an 80 ft light steel tower built in 1922
evidence.quote: Cashel (80 ft. light steel), Wicklow (80 ft. light steel), Mt. St. Patrick (80 ft. light steel), Myer's Cave (80 ft. light steel), Methuen (wooden) and Matawatchan (80 ft. light steel) Towers were built in 1922.

evidence.supports: The Tweed district list heading gives 1922 as the year the district was formed
evidence.quote: Tweed Fire District (Tower History Notes)- Formed in 1922

evidence.supports: The Tweed district was founded in 1922 by the former Ontario Department of Lands and Forests (now the MNR)
evidence.quote: The Tweed Forest Fire District was founded by the former Ontario Department of Lands and Forests (now the MNR) in 1922

evidence.supports: The district's headquarters served as the central hub for 21 fire lookout towers
evidence.quote: It was the central headquarters for 21 fire lookout towers

evidence.supports: The district's headquarters on Hungerford Road in Tweed served as the hub for 21 lookout towers
evidence.quote: The headquarters for the district were housed at Hungerford Road in town.

evidence.supports: Each tower took compass bearings on a fire it spotted and relayed them by radio to headquarters
evidence.quote: When a fire was spotted in the forest a towerman would get the degree bearings from his respective tower and radio back the information to headquarters.

evidence.supports: During the 1970s every tower in the district was shut down as aerial methods took over
evidence.quote: However, in the 1970s all the towers had been decommissioned as aerial firefighting techniques were employed.

evidence.supports: The name matches Wicklow Township in the historic Hastings area
evidence.quote: Wicklow Twp. in historical HASTINGS Co.

evidence.supports: Wicklow Township is one of three northern townships in the historic Hastings area
evidence.quote: The townships of Bangor, Wicklow and McClure are the three most northerly

evidence.supports: Hastings Highlands was incorporated on 1 January 2001 when the Township of Bangor, Wicklow and McClure, Herschel and Monteagle were amalgamated; no source ties historic Wicklow Township to that merged township
evidence.quote: The current municipality of Hastings Highlands was incorporated on January 1, 2001, when the Township of Bangor, Wicklow and McClure, Township of Herschel, and Township of Monteagle were amalgamated.

evidence.supports: The fan-kept list covers towers still standing; it does not name Wicklow (absence checked by text search of the page, 2026-10-20)
evidence.quote: The Ontario MNR has decided, as of 2013, to remove many of these still standing towers.

evidence.supports: The index gives the location as Tweed, Ontario
The index says the tower is steel and appears on a 1977 Pembroke topographic sheet and a current fourth-edition map sheet; the index is the only site record and describes nothing standing at the site
evidence.quote: Steel. Appears on Pembroke topographic map 31F, 3rd ed., 1977; and on current 4th edition mapsheet.

sources.title: Ontario Fire Towers (Tweed Fire District tower history notes)

notes_for_editor: The build year (1922), the 80 ft height and the light-steel type come from one fan-site list (Geocities, Tweed Fire District notes). No register or official record was found to confirm them. Firelookout confirms only 'Steel' and two map sheets. The Wikipedia decommissioning sentence covers the whole Tweed district; it reaches Wicklow only because the fan list places Wicklow in that district. The fan list also says 'some of these towers were taken over by the Lindsay District in about the 1940s' without naming them, so Wicklow's status after that, and whether it was among the towers decommissioned in the 1970s, is unconfirmed. The index labels the location 'Tweed, Ontario', but its coordinates (45.31164, -77.94821) lie roughly 90 km north of Tweed village by my own estimate (not sourced), so the label may name the fire district rather than a town; check before publishing the location line. Hastings Highlands: the story now states only what the 2001 source says, that the Township of Bangor, Wicklow and McClure (with Herschel and Monteagle) was amalgamated into Hastings Highlands. No source ties the historic Wicklow Township to that merged township, so the link is a name match only, and the tower's location is not tied to the township at all. The fan-site still-standing list is undated (it mentions 2013) and its silence about Wicklow is weak evidence either way. No photos found. Access and visit facts are omitted because no source describes them. Search budget used: 2. Fact-check 2026-10-20: all 12 evidence quotes were found on the first run. The story body is about 194 words. Changes: the Hungerford Road headquarters claim was added as evidence (Wikipedia: 'The headquarters for the district were housed at Hungerford Road in town.'); the 'Tweed Forest Fire District' name in the first sentence was changed to 'Tweed Fire District' to match the cited source; the sentence that Wicklow Township itself became part of Hastings Highlands was replaced with the amalgamation the source states; the word 'County' was removed from the township sentence (the township is now described as in the historic Hastings area); and four sentences that copied source wording were reworded.
